extracted.intended_audience: readers and scholars of modern Russian history, propaganda studies, and the history of antisemitism
extracted.subtask_description: Critical/historical analysis of the origins, textual variants, dissemination, and political uses of the 'Protocols of the Elders/Wise Men of Zion' and related antisemitic forgeries. Focuses on methods for detecting fabrication and political manipulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Textual consistency across versions
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare different published versions (Nilus, Lutostansky, Butmi, Retcliffe-Goedsche) for additions, deletions, and changes in wording and claims—e.g., Nilus adding '929 years before the birth of Christ', transformation of 'the sages' into 'the government of the Jews', and Butmi's change from future-terror to past-assassination phrasing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine parallel passages, note chronological changes (pre- and post-revolution edits), and treat abrupt insertions or politically convenient alterations as strong evidence of fabrication or later tampering. Use side-by-side comparisons and document how changes serve political aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provenance and authorship verification
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish who vouched for or first published the documents (e.g., Sergius Nilus, Lutostansky, Butmi), and whether these publishers were associated with known political groups (Black Hundreds, Russian secret police).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trace original publication contexts, publishers, and any institutional links. Suspicious provenance (single partisan source, secretive circulation, ties to agitprop organizations) reduces credibility. Photographic reproductions and publisher indicia should still be checked against independent records.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use (or non-use) by contemporary authorities
rubrics_metrics.description: Check whether contemporaneous actors who would plausibly rely on such documents (e.g., prosecutors in major related trials like the Beilis case) actually used them as evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absence of reliance on the documents by those seeking to make the same political point suggests the documents were not considered credible even by partisan actors; include review of trial records, official correspondence, and internal memos.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plausibility and mainstream editorial reception
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether mainstream editors, translators, or publishers omitted or rejected parts because they seemed 'too absurd' or unbelievable for their audience (example: American editors omitting parts of Nilus's epilogue).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether reputable presses or editors declined to print certain claims; mainstream rejection is a heuristic for implausibility, though not definitive. Note when material is deliberately edited to suit local sensibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual/political motive analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the documents align with or serve the political aims of specific actors or regimes (e.g., the Tsarist government's desire to discredit England and the Jews, employment of Black Hundreds as agitprop).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place texts within historical events (revolution periods, post-armistice chaos). If textual changes or circulation patterns map onto political needs (e.g., to justify pogroms or to discredit opponents), treat this as evidence of instrumental fabrication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dissemination networks and financial/propaganda incentives
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze how the texts spread (countries, periodicals, emigrant agents) and the motives of those spreading them (commercial gain, political activism, loss of prior patronage as with Black Hundreds émigrés seeking income).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map publication dates, languages, and outlets; look for repeated republication by the same networks or for anonymous embellishers. Financial or opportunistic motives for spread weaken claims of authenticity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhetorical and conspiratorial techniques as red flags
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify common propaganda devices used in the texts: scapegoating a minority, attributing world events to secret plans, invoking ancient prophecy or symbolic parallels (e.g., connecting Anglo-Saxons to Israelites), and moralistic character attacks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat sweeping conspiracy narratives, symbolic analogies presented as evidence, and selective historical parallels with skepticism. Flag passages that universalize a group's 'traits' or that use pseudo-historical etymologies and heraldic associations as evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary-source corroboration and documentary evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Seek independent primary documents (letters, official records, photographed facsimiles) that corroborate claims—e.g., the reproduced letter from Grand Duke Michael to Lutostansky shown in the book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authenticate such supporting documents separately (provenance, archival records, paper/ink dating where possible). Even supportive primary items must be evaluated for context and possible forgery or misattribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal contradictions and implausible chronological claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Spot internal logical contradictions or historically implausible assertions (such as a political plan devised '929 years before the birth of Christ') and use them as indicators of fabrication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-check historical claims with established scholarship and timelines; mark manifest anachronisms or numerically specific but unsupported claims as warning signs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resilience to critical scrutiny
rubrics_metrics.description: Test whether the assertions survive open analysis—'A lie shuns the sunlight... It cannot survive analysis.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply rigorous textual criticism, cross-referencing, and publication-history study; document where claims fail under scrutiny. Use cumulative weight of inconsistencies, provenance issues, and rhetorical devices to evaluate authenticity.
